The architecture RFC evaluated replacing our polling-based transactional outbox pattern with Debezium change data capture for publishing order events to Kafka. In the legacy design, 24 worker instances polled an outbox table every 500 milliseconds. Under peak load of 15000 transactions per second, outbox table contention generated 80% CPU utilization on the primary Postgres database and introduced 900 milliseconds of end-to-end event latency.

By adopting Debezium with Postgres pgoutput logical decoding, the CDC connector reads change events directly from the write-ahead log without querying database tables. This eliminated polling read amplification and dropped event propagation latency down to 40 milliseconds across 32 Kafka topic partitions.

However, the CDC architecture introduced new operational trade-offs around write-ahead log disk retention. If the Kafka connector stalls, inactive replication slots block Postgres from recycling WAL segments, which can consume 120 gigabytes of disk storage within 3 hours. We mitigated this by configuring slot max size limits and alert thresholds on replication lag.

Our distributed tracing RFC addressed trace context fragmentation across our polyglot microservices fleet. The legacy architecture used Zipkin B3 propagation headers across 48 backend services written in Go, Java, and Python. Edge ingress proxies dropped B3 headers when translating incoming HTTP requests to internal gRPC calls, causing 35% of distributed traces to lose parent context.

We migrated service telemetry to the W3C TraceContext standard using traceparent and tracestate headers. During the transition phase, our telemetry interceptors operated in dual-header mode by reading incoming B3 or W3C headers and writing both standards downstream across 64 edge and worker microservices.

This resolved context propagation loss without breaking legacy clients. We also calibrated the adaptive trace sampling rate to 5% across all gateway routes. This reduced telemetry storage ingestion by 400 gigabytes per day and stabilized collector latency at 12 milliseconds.

The caching infrastructure RFC evaluated shard partitioning algorithms for our distributed cache tier under high node churn. Our production cluster runs 128 cache instances serving 450000 read requests per second. With legacy consistent hashing using single token positions, hash key distribution produced 40% memory skew, causing several cache node points to exhaust memory and evict hot session keys prematurely.

We benchmarked consistent hashing rings configured with 256 virtual node points against rendezvous hashing. The virtual node topology balanced key distribution across instances and reduced memory allocation skew down to 3%. However, client drivers had to maintain a synchronization ring of 32768 virtual node tokens, which increased ring lookup CPU overhead during frequent cluster rebalances.

Rendezvous hashing delivered uniform key allocation without maintaining any shared ring state in client memory. However, calculating independent hash weights for all 128 node targets on every request increased client routing overhead to 800 microseconds. The architectural committee approved consistent hashing with virtual node points because sub-millisecond lookup speed remained our primary latency objective.

Our storage engine RFC benchmarked LSM-tree architectures against B-tree engines for our telemetry ingestion pipeline. The workload ingests 80000 time-series metrics per second. Under B-tree storage engines like Postgres, random updates to unaligned disk leaf pages generated a write amplification factor of 35. However, concurrent background compaction cycles created severe disk IO contention. During Level 0 to Level 1 compaction passes, tail read latency surged from 4 milliseconds to 65 milliseconds.

The RFC team adopted RocksDB with partitioned block indexes and bloom filters configured at 10 bits per key. We isolated write-ahead logs on dedicated physical solid-state drives and capped compaction write bandwidth at 150 megabytes per second. This stabilized read performance and maintained write amplification below 5 without compaction latency spikes.

Our system architecture RFC resolved broken trace causality across our asynchronous event-driven pipelines. When Debezium streamed change data capture records from Postgres into Kafka, downstream consumers lost upstream distributed trace context. Because database write-ahead log records omit HTTP and gRPC trace headers, over 70000 asynchronous billing events appeared as disconnected root spans in telemetry dashboards.

We redesigned the transactional outbox schema to persist W3C TraceContext fields inside the database table. When microservice endpoints process incoming requests, they capture the active traceparent header and write it alongside the domain event in a single database transaction. We then deployed a custom Debezium single message transform that extracts traceparent attributes and injects them into Kafka record headers.

This pipeline restored end-to-end distributed trace correlation across 50 downstream consumer services. Under a benchmark load of 20000 events per second, the Debezium header transformation added only 2 milliseconds of pipeline latency. The design maintained complete trace visibility across asynchronous boundaries without degrading primary database transaction throughput.
